49b03748cf:
This chapter is about making an agent follow rules that must always hold. It sets programmatic enforcement (prerequisite gates and hooks) against prompt guidance. It covers the Agent SDK hook mechanism, which intercepts tool calls and normalises tool results. It also covers structured handoffs to humans, and how to decompose requests that carry several concerns.

It's built on one official sample question: an agent that skips get_customer in 12% of conversations. Every mechanism is shown as running code with real traces, then mapped to servlet filters, AOP and saga guards from Java/Spring.
d1fd234e37:
The whole chapter rests on two sentences.

A prompt changes the probability that the model does the right thing; code decides whether the wrong thing can happen at all, so any rule that must hold on every request belongs in a hook or a gate that runs before the tool executes, not in the system prompt.

The same interception point serves four jobs: block a call that violates policy (and tell the model what to do instead), rewrite the call's arguments, normalise the tool's result before the model reads it, and hand the case to a human with a structured summary when the agent must stop.
5d82767bdb:
Everything in this chapter follows from those two sentences.

The first one explains why the official sample question has one correct answer. A support agent skips get_customer in 12% of conversations and issues refunds against the wrong account. Rewording the prompt, adding few-shot examples, switching to a larger model: all of these make the 12% smaller. None of them makes it zero. For a rule about money and identity, "smaller" isn't an acceptable engineering answer.

A prerequisite that blocks process_refund until a verified customer id exists makes the failure impossible, not just unlikely.
e0d844f419:
The second sentence describes the Agent SDK's hook system, which is what task statement 1.5 asks you to know. A hook is a function the runtime calls at a fixed point in the tool-call lifecycle.

  • PreToolUse runs before the tool. It can allow, deny, ask a human, or rewrite the input.
  • PostToolUse runs after the tool returns. It can replace what the model sees, add context, or record state.

Task statement 1.4 adds two patterns around the enforcement. The structured handoff covers what a human needs when the agent escalates. Decomposition covers what to do when one message holds three problems.
699d7551f5:
The official knowledge points for the two task statements are short, so here they are in full.

For 1.4:

  • the difference between programmatic enforcement (hooks, prerequisite gates) and prompt-based guidance;
  • when deterministic compliance is required, prompt instructions have a non-zero failure rate;
  • structured handoff protocols for human escalation (customer details, root cause analysis, recommended actions);
  • decomposing multi-concern requests into distinct items handled in parallel.

For 1.5:

  • PostToolUse hooks that normalise heterogeneous data formats (dates, status codes) before the model processes them;
  • tool-call interception hooks that block policy violations, such as refunds above a limit, and redirect to an escalation workflow;
  • choosing hooks over prompts when the business rules need guaranteed compliance.

The rest of the chapter teaches each of these from the ground up. It adds the operational detail the exam scenarios lean on: matchers, JSON in and out, permissionDecision, exit code 2, updatedInput, ordering, latency, idempotency, state, failure modes and testing. And it shows the Java/Spring parallels as it goes.
50166486e9: None of this was invented for language models. Enforcing a rule on every call, in a place the caller can't skip, is one of the oldest ideas in computer security. The vocabulary of hooks, interceptors and guards comes from systems you've already built.
02f61f41bc:
The 1972 Anderson report for the US Air Force defined the reference monitor. It's a component that mediates every access by a subject to an object, can't be bypassed, and is small enough to verify.

Saltzer and Schroeder's 1975 paper named the design principle complete mediation: every access to every object must be checked for authority.

Both rest on one assumption. The party being checked isn't trusted to check itself. A process doesn't decide whether it may open a file; the kernel does.
6d77ab7fff:
An LLM agent is the same situation with a new kind of subject. The model chooses which tool to call and with which arguments, and you don't control that choice.

A prompt that says "always verify the customer first" asks the subject to police itself. A PreToolUse hook is the reference monitor. It sits on the only path between the model's request and the tool.
579aa0e730:
Garcia-Molina and Salem's 1987 paper "Sagas" tackled long-lived business transactions that can't hold a database lock for hours. A saga splits the work into steps, each with a compensating action. An orchestrator makes sure the steps run in a legal order, and undoes them in reverse if a later step fails.

If you built order management for a carrier, you've written this: RESERVE_NUMBER before ACTIVATE_SIM before START_BILLING, with a guard on every transition and a compensation for every step.

A prerequisite gate is a saga guard; section 11 draws the refund workflow as one. The lineage also explains why PostToolUse can't prevent harm. Once the step has run, all you can do is compensate.
2d2061788f:
Kiczales and colleagues introduced aspect-oriented programming in 1997. It handles cross-cutting concerns (logging, security, transactions) that otherwise get copy-pasted into every method. AspectJ (2001) made it practical in Java, and Spring AOP (Spring 1.0, 2004) put @Around advice in front of ordinary beans.

In parallel, the Servlet 2.3 specification (2001) added filters: a chain of components that see every request before the servlet does, and can reject it. Spring MVC's HandlerInterceptor and Spring Security's filter chain follow the same shape. Express middleware and Kubernetes admission webhooks are the same pattern elsewhere.
586cebaccd:
All of them settled on the contract hooks use today:

  • a pointcut or matcher selects which calls the component sees;
  • the component receives the call and its context;
  • it returns a decision: proceed, reject, or proceed with a modified request;
  • a post-phase can transform the response.

Where hooks differ from a servlet filter chain is ordering. A filter chain is sequential, ordered by @Order. The Agent SDK runs matching hooks concurrently and combines their decisions (section 09).
bea4ba94e3:
Enterprise access control split the reference monitor into two roles. The XACML standard (OASIS, 2003) calls them the policy enforcement point (PEP) and the policy decision point (PDP). The PEP intercepts the request and enforces the answer. The PDP evaluates rules and returns permit or deny.

A PreToolUse hook is a PEP. The function inside it that checks "is this refund over the limit for this verified customer" is the PDP. Keeping them separate pays off twice. You can test the decision as a pure function (section 10), and you can swap the enforcement location (section 04) without rewriting the rules.

In the telecom estate you work in, the PEP is the API gateway in front of the order and billing services. It authenticates, rate-limits and rejects non-conforming calls before the backend sees them. No backend team relies on callers being polite.
1cb3a04cb9:
Michael Nygard's Release It! (2007) popularised the circuit breaker, and Netflix Hystrix and Resilience4j carried it into Spring services. A breaker is a stateful guard. It refuses calls once a condition is met (too many failures), and tells the caller why, so the caller can fall back.

A prerequisite gate has the same anatomy: state that persists across calls, a rule that flips from allow to refuse, and a structured refusal the caller is expected to act on. The difference is the trigger. A breaker opens on observed failure. A gate stays closed until a precondition is observed.

In both, the refusal carries a reason code. A guard that fails silently leaves the caller guessing, and that's the anti-pattern section 14 calls silent denial.
07015fdb96:
When function calling let models act, the early controls were prompt-level rules and output-validation libraries (Guardrails AI and NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails, both 2023). These check the text of a response. But an agent's risk lies in its actions, so the useful interception point moved from the output to the tool call.

Claude Code shipped hooks in 2025: user-defined shell commands that run at lifecycle events, such as before and after a tool call, configured in a settings file. The Claude Agent SDK exposes the same events as in-process callbacks. The two forms share one JSON contract, which is why the exam treats them as one topic.
0dbf21f6f4:
The second half of 1.4 comes from healthcare and contact centres. Patients get harmed at the moment care passes from one clinician to another, when context is lost. The SBAR format (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) came out of US Navy practice and was adapted for hospitals in the early 2000s.

Contact centres reached the same conclusion. The L1/L2/L3 support tiers and the "warm transfer" exist because making a customer repeat their problem is the failure.

The exam's three handoff elements (customer details, root cause analysis, recommended actions) are SBAR with different labels. The receiving human hasn't read the conversation, so the handoff must stand alone.
153ca09da7:
Why does the exam insist that prompt instructions have a non-zero failure rate? Look at what a prompt is.

A system prompt is text in the context window. The model generates its next action by sampling from a probability distribution. That distribution is conditioned on all of that text, on the conversation so far, on the tool results, and on its training.

An instruction such as "ALWAYS call get_customer before lookup_order" shifts the distribution a long way. A well-trained model follows a clear instruction very often. But the output is still a sample. A distribution that puts 99.5% on the right action puts 0.5% somewhere else.
914e3300d3:
Four things push the real number up from the ideal, and they're worth naming in an exam answer.

  • Context dilution: after thirty turns and several large tool results, the instruction is a small part of what the model attends to.
  • Competing signals: a customer who says "I'm in a hurry, just refund order 8812" supplies a plausible reason to skip a step.
  • Input you do not control: tool results and user messages can contain text that looks like instructions.
  • Drift across releases: a prompt tuned for one model snapshot behaves differently on the next. The failure rate is a moving target you have to re-measure.
86778ca19e:
A rate that sounds negligible per conversation isn't negligible at volume.

Say the model skips verification in 12% of conversations, as in the official sample. Then ten conversations contain at least one skipped verification with probability 1 - 0.8810, about 72%.

Now suppose you improve the prompt until the skip rate is 0.5%. A carrier handling 20,000 care conversations a day, with refunds in a fifth of them, would still see roughly 20 conversations a day in which a refund path ran without verification. Each one is a refund to the wrong account, a privacy incident, or both.

Rules also compound. Five independent rules, each followed 99% of the time, are all followed in only 0.995 of conversations, about 95%.
73a3e2d480:
A rule can be enforced in four places.

  • In the context (system prompt, few-shot examples, tool descriptions), it's a request, and compliance is a probability.
  • In the harness (the loop that executes tools, a hook, a gate), it's code that runs between the model's request and the tool. That makes it a guarantee for every call that passes through that point.
  • In the tool itself, it's a guarantee for that tool only.
  • In the service, it's a guarantee for every client, including ones that never heard of the agent.

A payments-grade design uses more than one. The hook gives the model a fast, specific reason and keeps the conversation on track. The service is the last line if the hook is misconfigured. Example 19_enforcement_options_compared.py measures that claim (section 04).
c371c94efe:
This isn't an argument against prompts. Prompts carry judgment that code can't: how to phrase an apology, when to offer a goodwill credit, which of three plausible plans to recommend. They also cut how often the model hits a gate at all, which saves round trips.

The rule of thumb for the exam is short. Use code for invariants and prompts for judgment.

When a question describes a rule with words such as "always", "never", "must", "compliance", "regulatory" or "financial", the answer is code. When it describes tone, prioritisation or phrasing, the answer is a prompt.
5d72427221:
The official sample question describes a customer-support agent with four tools: get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund and an escalation tool. The system prompt says to verify the customer first.

Production logs show that in about 12% of conversations, the agent calls lookup_order or process_refund without ever calling get_customer. In some of those, it acts on whatever account the order id points to. That's the wrong account when the customer typed the wrong order number, or when two customers share a name.

The question asks which change is most effective. The right answer is a programmatic prerequisite: block lookup_order and process_refund until get_customer has returned a verified customer id.
061e7a0484:
Companion example 01_prompt_only_baseline.py reproduces the failure on 1,000 simulated conversations. The model is a scripted policy that reads tool results and recovers from errors like the real one, with a knob for the skip rate.

Two customers named Maria Lopez exist (accounts C-5531 and C-7102). And 20% of conversations quote an order that belongs to the other one.
2c99cde3f4:
In the second row, 104 conversations skipped verification. Of those, 64 went on to refund with no verification at all, and 19 refunded the wrong account. The third row is a 98%-obedient model, and it still produces eight unverified refunds.

The "over-limit" column is a second prompt rule: "refunds above 500.00 must be escalated". It's forgotten in 5% of conversations. Nothing enforces it, so 18 refunds of 640.00 or 799.00 went out that should have gone to a human.
14749c5ade:
Start with the smallest possible implementation. The idea is simple, and hooks are just a packaging of it.

The loop from chapter 1 gets one new piece of state and one new check. The state is a dictionary owned by the harness, never by the model. The check sits between "the model asked for a tool" and "the harness executed it".
c14f980630: State is derived from tool results, not from model text. The harness sets verified_customer only when it sees a successful get_customer result with found: true. If the model writes "I've verified your account" in prose, nothing changes. It's the same principle as chapter 1's rule: stop_reason is a structured field, and the wording of a reply isn't.
017e5e1502: The refusal is an is_error tool result that tells the model what to do. It doesn't raise, and it doesn't return an empty string. The loop continues, and the model reads the message like any other tool output. Chapter 1's fifth exam scenario showed what happens when a failure is hidden from the model. Here the failure is shown on purpose, with a recovery instruction.
c144dc31a8: Every call passes through the check. The gate isn't a suggestion in a tool description. Whatever the model asks for goes through the same branch, including parallel calls in the same turn.
a316902033: Now trace a conversation in which the model skips the step. The customer writes "Refund ORD-330915 please, I'm maria.lopez@example.com". The scripted model, configured with skip_verify=True, goes straight to the order. Here's what the harness did.
092310167f: Read the third line. The first call the model made, lookup_order, never executed. The executed list starts with get_customer. In between, the model received the denial, understood it, and did the right thing. On the wire, the second request in that conversation looked like this.
e1e3e178e4:
Nothing about this request is special. It's an ordinary tool_use with its paired tool_result, flagged as an error.

The gate is invisible to the API and fully visible to the model. That's why a deny reason must be written for the model to act on. The next turns are get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund. The skipped step cost one extra model call.
d0385ee1df: Run 1,000 conversations at the official 12% skip rate, and 125 skip verification. The gate leaves refund without verification=0 and wrong-account refunds=0.
14c8b7a337:
A gate that records only "someone was verified" has a hole. The model can verify Maria Lopez C-5531, then call process_refund with customer_id: "C-7102".

The state must hold the verified value, and later calls must be checked against it (section 06 shows the ACCOUNT_MISMATCH hook). It's the rule that stops a logged-in user from editing someone else's record by changing an id in the URL. Authentication isn't authorisation, and the second check needs the first one's result.
5978751291:
Several other mechanisms look like gates. Each covers part of the problem, and the exam likes to offer them as distractors, so know where each one stops.

Example 19_enforcement_options_compared.py runs them on the same 1,000 conversations. The columns count refunds issued without verification, refunds to the wrong account, and refunds above the limit.
878db301c2:
Notice what the measured table says about completeness. Mechanisms B, C and D each fix the verification column and leave the limit column at 18. A mechanism that covers one rule isn't an enforcement strategy.

The hook is attractive because verification, ownership, limits and handoff validation can all live at one interception point, in code you can review and test.
6612549c9c:
A hook is a function the runtime calls at a fixed point in the agent's lifecycle. The runtime passes it a JSON description of what's about to happen, or has just happened. The hook answers with a JSON decision.

That's the entire mechanism. The detail lies in which events exist, how a hook is selected, what it receives, and what its answer can change.
35608019c6: An event fires. The model has emitted a tool_use block, and the runtime is about to execute it. That's a PreToolUse event.
4a7ac7b415: Matching hooks run, concurrently. Each one receives the event JSON. An SDK callback is an async function. A settings hook is a process that reads the JSON from stdin.
bb8760e490: The model sees the effect, not the hook. A denial becomes a tool result. A rewritten result replaces the real one. The Messages API contract of chapter 1 doesn't change.
b678db34b4: Claude Code defines many events. The Agent SDK exposes a subset as callbacks, and the Python and TypeScript SDKs differ. Here are the ones this chapter uses, with current availability from the SDK documentation.
3320a5ecd9: For 1.4 and 1.5, the two that matter are PreToolUse and PostToolUse. The exam text says "tool-call interception hooks" and "PostToolUse hooks". If an option proposes the wrong one for the job, that's usually the point of the question.
46ded024dd: A matcher is a string tested against the event's target. For tool events, the target is the tool name, and only the name. A matcher can't say "refund amount above 500"; checking arguments is code inside the hook. The matching rules from the Claude Code documentation are:
9d246abb8d: Tools from MCP servers are named mcp__<server>__<tool>. To match every tool of a server, you need mcp__support__.*. The bare prefix mcp__support__ is treated as an exact name, and it matches nothing.
abda5cb8b8:
Example 03_hook_contract_tour.py prints the full table. Here's the line to remember. A gate registered with the matcher process_refund never fires for the tool the model sees as mcp__support__process_refund. It looks just like a gate that always allows (section 10 catches it at startup).

The opposite mistake also bites. A regex like Edit.* that's slightly too broad guards tools you didn't mean to.
3d6afea48f: Every hook receives the same envelope, plus event-specific fields. Here's a real PreToolUse input, as captured by example 03. The fields come from the SDK's PreToolUseHookInput type. The runtime adds a few more fields over time, so read the ones you need and ignore the rest.
d179260dc0:
session_id is the key for all state a hook keeps (section 09). tool_use_id is the same id as the API's tool_use.id, and it's the natural key for idempotency. When a hook fires inside a subagent, agent_id and agent_type are added.

A PostToolUse input adds tool_response, the tool's output. Its exact shape depends on the tool: a plain object, a string, or an MCP-style list of text blocks. Log one real payload from your SDK version before writing a parser. And write the parser to accept all three (companion helper extract_json).
c3b6f793a0:
In the Python SDK, a callback has the signature async def hook(input_data, tool_use_id, context). The third argument is reserved for future use.

A callback returns a dictionary. Returning {} means "no opinion". That's not the same as returning an explicit allow, and the difference matters in the next subsection.
943a212d5f: The output has two layers. Top-level fields are accepted on every event. hookSpecificOutput carries the fields that belong to the event, and it must include hookEventName.
f4d4077914:
The four permissionDecision values work like this.

  • allow lets the call proceed, and also skips the user permission prompt. With the SDK's can_use_tool callback, a hook's allow means the callback isn't consulted either. So don't return allow when you only mean "I have no objection".
  • deny blocks the call and sends the reason to the model.
  • ask escalates to a person through the normal permission flow.
  • defer ends the turn with a result whose stop_reason is "tool_deferred". The call can then be resumed later, for example after an out-of-band approval.

When several hooks answer, the most restrictive result wins, in the order deny, then defer, then ask, then allow. A single deny blocks the call, whatever the others said.
3f1e608ab3:
Two more rules belong with this table.

First, on settings-based command hooks, exit code 2 blocks the action even if the JSON on stdout says allow. Section 08 covers exit codes.

Second, what updatedInput does depends on the decision it's paired with. With allow, it auto-approves the rewritten call. With ask, it shows the rewrite to the user. With no decision, the call still goes through normal permission evaluation. With defer, it's ignored. Return a new object rather than editing tool_input in place.
b8533a397a:
The Agent SDK for Python drives the Claude Code CLI as a subprocess. When you register callbacks, the SDK sends the CLI a list of hook registrations with callback ids during initialisation.

When an event matches, the CLI sends the SDK a control request of type hook_callback, carrying the callback id and the event JSON. The SDK looks up your function, awaits it, and sends the returned dictionary back. On the way, it translates async_ and continue_ to async and continue.

You can see the flow in the installed package source: claude_agent_sdk/_internal/query.py, with the types in claude_agent_sdk/types.py.
f64d35fb70:
Two consequences follow.

Your hook runs in your process, with direct access to your databases, caches and application objects. That's why SDK hooks are the right choice for an application that owns the session.

And every hook invocation is a round trip over a local control channel. A callback is cheap, but not free (section 09 measures it).

If a callback raises, the SDK sends an error response for that control request. What the CLI then does with a failed policy hook is the kind of detail that changes between releases. So the safe design doesn't rely on it: catch exceptions inside the hook and return an explicit deny (section 10).
a2c3947d1c:
Task statement 1.5 names the second job of hooks: tool-call interception that blocks policy violations, such as refunds above a threshold, and redirects to an escalation workflow. The pattern has four parts.

  • The hook is registered for the tool by name.
  • It reads the proposed arguments.
  • It decides using a rule and, where needed, session state.
  • When it refuses, it says what to do instead. The conversation then moves to the escalation path instead of dead-ending.
9a46762abb: Here are the three policy hooks from the companion library, with the state helpers they use. They have the exact signature the Agent SDK expects, so example 16 registers the same functions with the real SDK.
58d6a6928e: Registration is a dictionary from event name to a list of matchers. The gate's matcher is a regular expression, because it covers two tools. The policy hook is registered for one tool, by its full MCP name.
8c740b1939: The state-recording hook is a PostToolUse on get_customer, and the gate is a PreToolUse on the later tools. Separating them is deliberate. They run at different moments, with a model turn between them, so there's no ordering problem (section 09 explains why that matters).
1398cb8c62: To see the redirect work, run the case the prompt-only agent got wrong: a verified customer, an order of 799.00, and a model that has forgotten the 500.00 rule. Companion example 04_pretooluse_policy.py produces this trace from the loop with the hooks above.
e3c16e16b0:
Step through it.

Calls 1 and 2 pass. In call 2, the +normalised marker means a PostToolUse hook rewrote the order result (section 07).

In call 3, the model asks for a 799.00 refund. The hook denies it, nothing reaches the payments service, and the reason text goes back as the tool error. The model reads "Call escalate_to_human with a recommended_action", and does exactly that in call 4.

The customer receives a truthful message with a ticket number. The refund ledger is empty.

Without the redirect text, the same denial would leave the model to guess. Some runs would apologise and stop. Some would retry with 499.99. And some would tell the customer the refund went through.
64f19c6e28: Here's the aggregate result over 1,000 conversations, with the same 12% skip rate and a 5% rate of forgetting the limit:
d1c0c75278:
The hooks blocked 122 tool calls. Refunds fell from 434 to 397, because 37 refund attempts that shouldn't have happened became escalations. Now 603 go to humans, against 566 before.

That's the correct trade. Every blocked call was either unverified or broke a limit. Each one turned into an escalation the customer was told about, not a silent wrong refund.
9fb8ede910:
The reason is the only channel from your code to the model's next decision, so design it. A good reason has four parts:

  • a stable code the model can key on (REFUND_LIMIT);
  • the facts that triggered it (799.00 against 500.00);
  • a statement of whether to retry;
  • the next step, by name.
0ebe875652: Don't put secrets or internal thresholds into the reason, because the model can quote it. Keep the codes stable, because dashboards will count them.
4e00ed9024:
Not every policy is a hard no. A refund between 500.00 and 2,000.00 might be allowed with a supervisor's approval.

ask hands the decision to a person through the permission flow. defer parks the call by ending the turn with stop_reason: "tool_deferred", so an approval that takes hours can come back later and resume. In Spring terms, ask is step-up authentication or a maker-checker screen. defer is putting the command on a queue and answering with 202 Accepted.

The exam distinction: use deny when the rule is absolute, or when the next step is escalation by the agent. Use ask or defer when a person can say yes to this exact call.
ab0c6fb9a1:
Four rules keep rewriting safe.

Return the whole input. Example 06 shows what fails when a hook returns only the field it changed.
4a7429f5f8: Rewrite only what does not change meaning. Canonical form, defaults and idempotency keys are safe. Clamping a 799.00 refund to 500.00 isn't. A request that policy says needs a human decision becomes a silent partial refund. The customer who asked for 799.00 gets 500.00 with no explanation, and the model is never told a limit exists. If the meaning has to change, deny and redirect.
a2de73e946: One rewriter per field. Two hooks that both return updatedInput run concurrently, and the winner depends on completion order. The example engine flags the conflict. The real runtime doesn't promise an order, so check the docs and avoid the situation.
14f72f6ab5:
The third job in task statement 1.5 is the PostToolUse hook that normalises heterogeneous data formats (dates, status codes) before the model processes them.

This is a different problem from enforcement. Nothing here violates a rule. The tool worked. The problem is that its result is hard for a model to use reliably, and the model's mistakes are silent.
215c5f5401: A carrier's order data rarely lives in one system. In the companion domain, orders come from a legacy order-management system, a newer commerce platform, and the billing system. They describe the same fact in three ways: an order placed on 14 March 2026, and delivered.
3b939e690c:
A date is 03/14/2026, or an ISO timestamp with a zone, or the integer 1773483751. A status is the integer 3, the string "DELIVERED", or the letter "D". A price is an integer in cents, a string in dollars, or a float.

A capable model can usually read all of these. "Usually" is the problem. The task the model is doing with the data ("is this order inside the 30-day window?") involves date arithmetic, and the failure modes are subtle:

  • 03/04/2026 is 4 March in a US system and 3 April in a European one;
  • status 3 means delivered in one system, and may mean cancelled in another;
  • a model that reads cents as dollars approves a 100-times-too-large refund.

These errors don't raise exceptions. They produce a confident wrong answer.
ffba3983c5: Keep the transformation as a pure function with no framework types, so you can unit-test it with no SDK present. Make the hook a thin wrapper around it.
cc04a8c686: All three shapes now become the same object. Companion example 05 prints them side by side.
dea9c5aee2: Unknown shapes are reported, not guessed. When a fourth system appears with an unfamiliar payload, the hook leaves the raw data alone and adds additionalContext saying normalisation failed. The model is told not to infer dates from it, and the failure shows up in logs. A hook that tries to be clever with an unknown format just reproduces the model's silent-error problem in code.
208605efc5: The transformation is idempotent. Feed canonical data back in, and it passes through (normalise(normalise(x)) == normalise(x), printed as True in the example). Hooks can be delivered more than once (section 09), and a non-idempotent normaliser would raise on the second pass.
18eea0d365: Normalising drops fields. The raw legacy record had item, the platform record had lineItems, and the billing record had desc. The canonical shape has none of them. That was a decision: the refund workflow doesn't need them. If a later task does, add them to the canonical schema and to the three mappings together. Don't pass raw payloads through "just in case", because that reopens the problem.
677bc570dd: Move arithmetic into code. The best normalisation also computes what the model would otherwise derive. Add days_since_order from the canonical date and today's date, and the model compares a number with 30 and never subtracts dates. The same reasoning applies to currency conversion and time zones. The model is good at deciding what to do with a clean fact. It's unreliable at producing one from dialects.
0809d03620: Through the loop, the tool_result the model receives is the replacement, not the original. The API sees a normal result. Only your harness knows it was rewritten.
ed1038c551:
tool_response is whatever the tool produced, in the form the runtime hands over: a dict, a JSON string, or, for an MCP tool, a list of {"type": "text", "text": "..."} blocks. The companion helper extract_json accepts all of them, and example 05 checks each shape. Capture one real payload from your SDK version and assert on it in a test.

For built-in tools, a replacement that doesn't match the tool's output schema is rejected, and the original is kept. For MCP tools, check the docs for your version.
8b03910492: A normalising hook can time out or raise. When a PostToolUse hook exceeds its timeout, the documented behaviour is that the runtime keeps the original tool result and the turn continues. Example 08 shows the consequence.
f24d2529ca:
The model read the raw legacy record. Normalisation by hook fails open.

If the guarantee must hold, put the transformation inside the tool or the MCP server. That's code you own, on the call path. Keep the hook as a second layer. For data that's merely inconvenient, failing open is acceptable, but decide that on purpose.
815de2eb92:
The same hook point serves other jobs too. It can redact personal data, trim a 40,000-token payload to the fields the task needs, record state (the verified flag in section 04), and write an audit row.

In Spring terms, this is ResponseBodyAdvice, or @Around advice that rewrites the return value. @AfterReturning can observe the value, but it can't replace it.
c45024ddb2: The exam text says "Agent SDK hooks", while the Claude Code documentation talks about hooks in settings files. They're two registration styles for the same JSON contract. The exam may ask you to choose between them, or to read a snippet written in either style. The difference is where your logic runs and how it talks to the runtime.
61bc01f556: The companion folder has a complete one. The command is a script that reads the event JSON from stdin and blocks refunds above the limit.
4dad4fdd45:
The structure has three levels: an event name, a list of matcher groups, and under each group a list of handlers.

Hook entries from the user, project, local and managed levels are merged, not replaced. The same handler listed in several files runs once. Managed policy can set allowManagedHooksOnly to block all other hooks. And disableAllHooks in a user or project file can't switch off managed hooks. For a bank-style control that individual developers must not remove, that's the mechanism.

In an SDK application, settings-file hooks load only when the matching entry is enabled in setting_sources. Check the docs for the default in your version before assuming they do or don't apply.
8ee1c076ab: Example 09 runs three versions of the same guard, so the difference is visible. Each one is given a 799.00 refund.
bebc628b08:
The third line is the classic trap, and it's a trap because it looks right. A script author writes sys.exit(1) to signal "this is a violation", as every Unix tool does. For a hook, exit 1 means "the hook itself had a problem", and the tool runs. The guard detected the violation, then failed to stop it.

Policy hooks block with exit 2, or with a JSON deny on exit 0. If the script also prints JSON while exiting 2, the JSON is ignored, because exit 2 uses stderr.
c9ca8adce4:
One more difference, and it reverses between the two styles.

If a command hook on PreToolUse times out, the documentation says the tool call isn't blocked. It continues through the normal permission flow. So a stalled shell hook isn't a gate.

If an SDK callback on PreToolUse times out, the tool call doesn't run, and the model receives a tool result saying the hook didn't respond.

The SDK style fails closed on timeout. The command style fails open. Know which one you wrote.
cb55ecf430:
A scenario that says "Agent SDK" or "an agent your team builds", or that needs the application's session data, wants an SDK callback. One that says "Claude Code", "team settings", or describes an organisation-wide control wants a settings hook (managed settings for the strongest version).

Either way, a question about which hook blocks is answered by the decision (deny or exit 2), never by the logging kind.
e780dc9391: One hook is easy to reason about. Real agents register several: a gate, a policy check, an audit logger, a normaliser. Four properties decide whether they work together. They run concurrently, they cost time, they can run more than once, and they need memory.
75c838f3c3:
When an event fires, all matching hooks run in parallel. The SDK's own documentation says it plainly: "all matching hooks run in parallel". Because completion order isn't deterministic, you should "write each hook to act independently rather than relying on another hook having run first".

This is a break from the servlet filter chain, where @Order fixes the sequence and each filter calls the next. It also means registration order carries no meaning. Registering the gate before the audit logger doesn't make the gate run first.
14b4897633: What the runtime does impose is a rule for combining answers. The most restrictive result wins, in the order deny, defer, ask, allow. Example 07 prints the matrix for every pair.
2c26ebd456:
A hook that returns {} has no opinion, so it never lowers the result.

This is also why the hook layer composes safely in one direction. You can add another restriction without reading the existing hooks, because an older allow can't undo a new deny.

It composes badly the other way. You can't add a hook that grants an exception to another hook's deny. Exceptions must go inside the denying hook.
893a465f19:
The classic mistake is a hook that quietly depends on another one. Hook A looks up the customer and stores it. Hook B reads that value to decide. B is registered after A, so it seems safe.

It isn't. Example 07 builds exactly this. A sleeps 50 ms to stand in for a database call, then writes state. B checks the state immediately.
fa14b81511:
There are three fixes, in order of preference.

  • Make hooks independent: each one reads what it needs from the event JSON or the session store, and none reads another hook's in-memory result.
  • Move the dependency across a model turn: this is what the gate does, with record_verified_customer as a PostToolUse on get_customer and prerequisite_gate as a PreToolUse on a later call. By the time the second runs, the first has finished.
  • Compose in one callback when the steps are inseparable. A single function that calls A then B has an order, because it's code.
18e6d77b1d:
One variant is easy to miss. Suppose the model requests get_customer and lookup_order together in one turn. If the runtime runs sibling calls concurrently, the gate for lookup_order may run before the PostToolUse of get_customer has recorded anything. So it denies.

That's the correct, fail-closed outcome. The model gets the error and retries in the next turn. It costs a round trip, and it never leaks. Test 14 asserts the invariant that matters: if lookup_order executed, the verification was already recorded.

(TypeScript also has a PostToolBatch event, which fires once per batch of parallel calls. It isn't available as a Python callback.)
fa2b488e1e: Every matching hook on a tool call sits on the critical path of that call. Concurrency means N hooks cost the slowest, not the sum: example 07 measures twenty 50 ms hooks at 52 ms total. But each hook is still added to every tool call it matches, and a conversation has many calls. Example 15 measures four kinds of hook on one machine.
7791e10a2f:
Model time dominates, so a well-written gate is invisible. The costs that do hurt are network calls inside a hot-path hook, and process start-up multiplied by many tool calls.

The measured numbers come from an offline engine that doesn't pay the SDK's control-channel round trip for each callback. Measure on your own deployment before quoting a figure. Practical guidance:
fc083f13b3: Keep gates on memory. Read a dictionary, a cache or the event JSON. If a check needs a remote call, cache the answer for the session, or move the check into the tool.
6d537bab25: Do side effects off the critical path. Logging and metrics can return async_: True (with an optional asyncTimeout), or hand the event to a queue. An async output can't block, modify or add context.
0dc874f888: Narrow the matcher, and set the timeout yourself with timeout= on the HookMatcher (in seconds). At the time of writing, the default has differed between releases, and between the package docstring (60) and the documentation (600).
2d53ab6f47:
A hook can see the same event more than once. A callback registered under two matchers that both match runs twice for one call. A control message can be retried. A resumed or replayed session re-fires events. A test harness may dispatch the same event repeatedly.

So a hook with a side effect must behave the same on the second delivery. The standard mistake is accumulating with +=.
32127d3098:
One 400.00 refund was recorded twice. The budget hook believed 800.00 was spent, and refused a legitimate second refund of 500.00.

The fix is the one you use for idempotent consumers on a message queue. Key every recorded fact by a natural id (here tool_use_id), store records, and recompute totals from the records.

The same discipline applies in two other places. The tool should take an idempotency_key, so a repeated process_refund is a no-op at the payments service; the PreToolUse hook can inject it (section 06). And the audit hook should upsert on (tool_use_id, event), so a replay doesn't create a second audit row.
2b559a22bb: A hook is a function with no memory. What it knows about the conversation arrives in the event: the session_id, the tool name and input, and, for PostToolUse, the response. Anything else (has this conversation verified a customer?) must come from a store you control. Example 10 walks through the design.
dd9b1e7e39: Key by session_id. A module-level variable is shared by every conversation in the process. Example 21 shows the result. After conversation A verifies Maria, conversation B, with a different customer, passes the gate without verifying. It's the agent version of storing the logged-in user in a servlet field instead of the HttpSession.
a0298e55e2: Sub-agents add agent_id to the input, with the same session_id. Decide per fact whether it belongs to the conversation (verification) or to one subagent (its own call budget). Store the verified id and a timestamp, not the whole customer record.
de813f1bd7: A gate has a second job beyond blocking: it must not fail silently. A gate that never fires looks exactly like a gate that always allows. A gate that crashes looks like one that was never there. This section covers the failure modes, and the tests that catch them.
5c15cc6cea:
Row 1 is the dangerous one. The session store is down, the gate raises, and the refund goes through.

The contract doesn't tell you what a raising callback does, so don't depend on the runtime's choice. Make the choice yourself, in the hook.
ac990f534a:
Fail closed is the right default for rules about money, identity and compliance. It has a cost, though: if the store is down, legitimate refunds stop. That's a decision for the business. Make it visible by alerting on the POLICY_CHECK_UNAVAILABLE code.

For hooks that only improve quality (a style normaliser), failing open is fine. The skill here is stating the policy for each hook and writing it down, not choosing one setting for all.
d59a22e35d:
Rows 6 and 7 show the quietest bug. The hook's logic is identical in both. But in row 6, it returns {"permissionDecision": "deny"} at the top level, where the runtime doesn't look. The refund executes.

The only defence is a test that feeds the hook a call it must block, and asserts the exact documented shape.
97e8d498cf: The most common production failure is a hook that doesn't match. Example 17 builds six registrations and runs the same refund through each.
d4555ef3f7:
The check is simple. Keep a list of tools that must be gated. At startup, assert that at least one PreToolUse matcher matches each one, and that every event key is a known event name. If not, fail the deploy.

In production, also alert if a gate shows zero evaluations over a period in which its tool was called. That's the runtime version of the same check.
0e40847fb5: Hooks are the part of the system that makes guarantees, so they get the most rigorous tests. They're also easy to test, because they're functions. Example 14 is a complete suite of 14 tests, in four layers.
9aaa20cafd: Unit tests call the callback directly with a hand-built input dict. No model, no SDK. A table drives the boundary: 500.00 passes, 500.01 is denied. State tests check that a not-found customer doesn't verify, and that sessions are isolated.
629fc894d9: Contract tests validate the output shape. A valid_shape() function encodes the documented rules. Decisions live inside hookSpecificOutput, which names its event. Values are one of four. Nothing that belongs inside sits at the top level. Run every hook output through it, plus a negative test that proves a wrong shape is rejected.
7459311678: Loop tests run a scripted model through the harness, and assert on side effects, not on the hook's return value. The blocked refund must be absent from the ledger and from the log of executed tools. The deny text the model received must contain the name of the next tool.
0ae2c94a53: Property tests fuzz the model. A fuzzing "model" issues random sequences of tool calls with random arguments, for 200 trials. The invariants must hold for all of them. No refund executes unless a get_customer executed before it. No refund goes above the limit. Every refund's customer id equals the verified id for that session.
437cc543b7: The two lines at the top are the sibling-call test. With sequential execution, the gate lets lookup_order through after get_customer records the verification. With concurrent execution, the gate runs first and denies. The test passes in both modes, because it asserts the invariant, not the order.
f147d88fb3:
The last test in the suite is a mutation check. It removes the gate and confirms that the dangerous refund then goes through. A test suite that can't fail proves nothing.

When you change a gate, mutate it: delete it, loosen the threshold, break the matcher. Then confirm some test goes red.
26c80ee663:
A single "verified" flag is the smallest state machine. Real processes have several states, and each tool is legal only in some of them.

If you've written a saga orchestrator for order management, you've already written the guard for this. The transition table says which steps are legal now. A guard can veto a structurally legal transition on a business rule. And an illegal event is rejected, not ignored.
eb1c2c298b:
One PreToolUse hook consults the table. One PostToolUse hook advances the state when a tool succeeds.

The model still chooses the path. The table decides only which steps are legal at this point, and a denial names the legal ones. This trace shows what the model sees across a conversation that tries to jump ahead.
785ba2b289: Call 6 deserves attention. After the refund succeeds, the state is REFUNDED, and process_refund isn't allowed in that state. So a duplicate refund request gets stopped by structure, not by luck, whether it comes from a model that didn't read the result or from a retried turn. The idempotency key at the payments service is the second line.
5294b59736:
In Java, this is Spring Statemachine. You get enums for states and events, and a Guard<S,E> for the rule that makes a legal transition illegal (the 500.00 limit). A hook maps "event not accepted" to deny (java/WorkflowGuard.java).

For the exam: a question may describe a multi-phase process ("a porting workflow with five phases") and ask how to make the phases happen in order. A programmatic gate or state machine is the answer. A longer prompt is the distractor.
ea78fe2cb5:
The second pattern in 1.4 is the handoff. Sometimes an agent can't or mustn't finish a case: a refund above its limit, a policy exception, a customer asking for a person, a failure the agent can't diagnose. Then it passes the case to a human.

The quality of that pass decides whether the human can act in thirty seconds, or must start the conversation again. The official elements are customer details, root cause analysis and recommended actions.
5bed91ff98:
Compare two escalations of the same case. The first is what a prompt-only agent typically produces: "Customer is upset about a refund, please help."

The human has to ask who the customer is, which order, what was checked, what the agent already told them, and what's wanted. The customer repeats everything. Second-contact resolution time rises. That's the exact failure contact-centre warm-transfer practice exists to avoid.
c6b2f5e923: The second is a structured handoff, the kind example 12 produces once the validation hook has done its work.
c0ebe1e466: The human can approve in one step. Everything above came from fields, so it can also be routed (by queue and amount), searched and measured.
e1ebebaa3f: Make the handoff the input schema of the escalation tool, so producing it is the only way to escalate. Four groups of fields carry the content.
110134eb94:
A schema alone doesn't make a handoff good. The model can fill every field with filler: root_cause: "too big", recommended_action: "help".

A PreToolUse hook on the escalation tool can check what the schema can't:

  • required fields are non-empty;
  • recommended_action is in the allowed set;
  • customer_id equals the verified customer;
  • an amount is present for refund decisions;
  • the root cause is long enough to act on.

If the handoff fails, the hook denies with the exact list of errors, and the model corrects it. Here are attempt 1 and attempt 2 from the example.
af65f2a8e7:
Facts the model shouldn't have to remember are better injected by code. The same example uses a second hook with updatedInput to fill evidence from the session's audit log, recording which tools actually ran. The model can't forget a check it made, or claim one it didn't.

The pattern generalises. The model supplies judgment (root cause, recommendation). The harness supplies facts (ids, amounts from tool results, what ran).
9cc2815d0f: Dump the transcript or send a free-text summary only. The human has to redo the root-cause analysis, and free text can't be validated, routed or aggregated.
edca1445bc: Handoff without a recommendation. The agent has seen the case. Withholding its best next step wastes that.
8e015a1d68: Escalating too early, or never. The limit gate decides when, and the schema decides what (Chapter 14 covers escalation criteria). Letting the model name the customer: take the id from the verified state instead.
c2ffcbd866:
The last knowledge point in 1.4 is decomposing multi-concern customer requests into distinct items, investigated in parallel, with a unified resolution.

A customer writes: "This is Maria. My April bill shows a $40 charge I don't recognise, my new Galaxy won't activate on the new line, and please cancel my old landline." That's three tasks, with different tools, different owners and different failure modes.
5a371c9fb3:
Handle it as one blob, and the loudest concern absorbs the answer while the others vanish. The model replies about the bill, never mentions the landline, and the customer calls back.

It's the same defect as the single-classifier decision tree in chapter 1: one decision made up front about a message that holds several.

The fix is structural. Extract the concerns into a list with ids. Run the independent ones in parallel. Track the status of each. Then write one reply that accounts for all of them.
e4e62b674f: Verify the shared prerequisite once. Identity applies to every item. Verify it before fan-out, and give every item the verified id. This is the gate from section 04, applied at the coordinator.
7c55c56781: Decompose into items with ids and a concern type, as structured output (a JSON schema, or a tool call that registers a work item). Validate the plan against the request: every concern the customer named should map to an item. Example 13 shows a check that catches a plan which leaves out the cancellation.
7670ae8c7d: Run independent items in parallel, dependent ones in order. A billing dispute and a device activation share nothing. Two writes to the same account record don't run concurrently. Each item can be its own loop or subagent with only its own tools, which also keeps context small (Chapter 2 covers coordinators and subagents).
2879190a4d: Merge by item. Collect each item's status with a per-item timeout and return_exceptions semantics, so one failure doesn't abort the others. The reply lists each item and its status, in plain language.
a2ce09c919:
The three outcomes cover every shape a real case produces.

  • I1 is escalated, and carries its own handoff (the structure from section 12, scoped to that item).
  • I2 failed. The customer-facing text doesn't leak the exception, while the internal field keeps it for operations.
  • I3 resolved.

The customer learns the state of all three, not just the one that succeeded. The wall time is the slowest item (0.45 s), not the sum (0.95 s): the usual benefit of parallel investigation.
c4ecb3c0d4:
Two links to other parts of the guide.

First, decomposition and parallel subagents are the subject of the next chapter's coordinator pattern. Here the point is the requirement to track items and answer all of them.

Second, hooks help in two places. The gate runs for each item's tool calls. And a Stop hook can refuse to let the agent finish while an item has no status. That turns "don't forget an item" from a prompt wish into a check.
37efae2e69: Each of these is a plausible implementation, which is why it shows up in exam options and in production code. Each one is shown with the broken code, the trace that exposes it, and the fix.
4b8af5ee18:
The temptation: the 12% skip rate is a prompt problem, so rewrite the prompt. Capitalise ALWAYS, add three few-shot examples, put the rule first and last.

Each change helps, and the numbers in section 03 show how much. What's broken is the claim that this finishes the job.
25812528f5:
Root cause. The rule is text in the context, and compliance is a probability. At 2%, the failure is eight unverified refunds in a thousand conversations.

Fix: a gate or PreToolUse hook (section 04). Keep the prompt too, so the model plans around the gate and rarely hits it.
95872ad971: The temptation: validate the refund in the hook that runs after the call, and "block" it there. The exam tests this by offering a PostToolUse hook as the option for a rule that must stop an action.
33f992cea6:
Root cause. By the time PostToolUse runs, the tool has executed.

Row 2 shows the ledger still holding the wrong-account refund; the "block" changed only what the model reads. Row 3 is a saga-style compensation: reverse the refund and tell the model. It repairs the data, but money moved and moved back, notifications went out, and the audit trail has two entries. Row 4 never lets it happen.

Fix: prevent with PreToolUse. Use PostToolUse to normalise, observe and record state, and to compensate for what you can't check in advance.
72387c2f09:
Root cause. The process serves many conversations. After A verifies, the variable stays set. B then passes the gate without verifying, and reads account data that isn't theirs.

Fix: store state by input_data["session_id"], in a durable store with a TTL (section 09).

This bug would pass every single-conversation test. That's why the suite has a multi-session test.
0e40eb3035:
A shell hook that follows Unix habit and exits 1 on a violation doesn't block. For hooks, exit 1 is a non-blocking error, and the refund proceeds (section 08, 09_command_hooks_exit_codes.py: refund_guard_buggy (exit 1) amount= 799.00 exit=1 -> allow). Fix: exit 2, or exit 0 with JSON deny, plus a test that runs the script with a violating input.

A hook registered for process_refund, when the runtime name is mcp__support__process_refund, never runs, and nothing reports it (17_matcher_pitfalls.py: BROKEN 1: bare tool name refund EXECUTED). Fix: use the qualified name or mcp__support__.*, plus the startup coverage check from section 10.
a09e1aa015:
A gate that blocks correctly but explains nothing turns a recoverable situation into a loop. The model asked for a refund and got an empty or generic failure. It has no way to know whether to retry, change the arguments or give up.

The usual result is the same call again, three or four times. Then comes an apology to the customer that blames a technical problem. The block was right. The denial just gave the model nothing to act on.
ec23b097c8:
Rule of thumb. A denial reason has three parts: a stable code the harness can count, the rule in one sentence, and the exact next action.

The "do not retry with a smaller amount" clause matters. Without it, a model will sometimes split 799.00 into two refunds of 399.50. That defeats the limit, the same way splitting a purchase defeats an approval threshold.

Count denials by code in your logs. A rising count for one code tells you which prompt or tool description is misleading the model.
80a0bef6d8:
Rewriting is legitimate for changes that don't alter meaning (section 07). It becomes an anti-pattern when the rewrite is invisible and the meaning does change.

The model reasons from what it believes it sent and received. If a hook rewrites the arguments or the result and says nothing, the model's picture of the world is wrong. Its next sentence to the customer will be wrong with it.
4470a70478:
Rule of thumb. A rewrite is safe when a third party, reading before and after, would say the two mean the same thing: a date in another format, a trimmed id, a default filled in. If they wouldn't, it's a decision, and decisions are denials.

When you do rewrite, use additionalContext to record what changed, so the model's account of events matches the system of record. Log the original and the rewritten value on the harness side as well. An audit that can't see the rewrite can't explain it.
1a08ff0eee: You've built every one of these before, under other names. The table maps the vocabulary. The companion folder has a runnable plain-JDK demo and three Spring files.
bed3b2f455: The file java/HookPipelineDemo.java needs only a JDK (17 or later; it compiles and runs on 21). It defines the two hook interfaces and a pipeline that combines decisions with "most restrictive wins". It also has the prerequisite gate, the refund limit, state recording, and an order normaliser. It fails closed when a hook throws.
69c902da8f: Your Spring service might execute the tools itself, either in your own agent loop or in an MCP server you host. If so, an aspect around the executor gives the same guarantee: no tool implementation can be called around it. The Redis template plays the part of the session store, and the catch block makes the failure policy explicit.
30b57a850a:
The last line of defence belongs where the data lives. A OncePerRequestFilter in front of POST /v1/refunds rejects an unverified, mismatched or over-limit refund with a typed error.

This is option D in the section 04 table. It protects every client, including ones that never used the agent's hooks. The harness maps its 409, 403 and 422 responses to is_error tool results.
ad0e081a3f:
In Java, the handoff schema is a record with Bean Validation annotations (@NotBlank, @Size(min = 20), an enum for recommendedAction). The violations become the model-facing error text.

Test it as you would the Python suite. Use JUnit 5 for each hook or advice, and @SpringBootTest with a mocked tool for the aspect. Add a seeded random-sequence test for the invariants, and a mutation test that removes the aspect and proves the guard test fails.
b86cc81679: Work each scenario before reading the reasoning. For 1.4 and 1.5, the wrong options are usually reasonable engineering ideas that are probabilistic, late, or aimed at the wrong layer.
b51096d448:
The rule must hold on every conversation, and the symptom is a measured non-zero failure rate. C is the only option that turns a probability into a guarantee. The downstream tools can't run without the prerequisite, and the error tells the model how to recover.

A and B lower the 12% (section 03 shows by how much), but can't reach zero. D has the same limitation at higher cost. It also doesn't address the root cause: the sequence isn't enforced anywhere.
9797dd32c4:
The hook runs before the side effect, and it can redirect the conversation. The deny reason becomes the tool error, and the model escalates.

A is prompt-level and probabilistic. C runs after the refund has been issued; it can flag, but not prevent. D is detection and compensation after the fact, and by then the customer has already been told the refund succeeded.

The requirement for a guarantee points to a hook. The requirement that the customer be told points to the redirect text.
40ed778a2f:
The problem is data the model receives, so the fix belongs on the result path, before the model reads it.

A leaves conversion and arithmetic to the model, and puts the knowledge in untested prose. C acts on the wrong side: the request was fine, and the response is the problem. D asks the same unreliable step to check itself.

B makes the transformation deterministic and testable. And a computed field removes date arithmetic from the model entirely.
54e9386388:
The official pattern is decomposition into distinct items, with a unified response. C resolves two items, escalates exactly the one that needs a person, and attaches the three handoff elements.

A and D drop work and push effort back onto the customer. B throws away what the agent completed, and makes the human do root-cause analysis from a transcript.
126f1e6f64:
PostToolUse fires after the tool succeeded. The refund exists by the time the hook runs, so "block" can change only what the model reads (section 14, anti-pattern 2). An async hook can't block anything at all.

A wouldn't change the ledger. D invents a problem. The symptom (the side effect occurred) points to timing, not matching.
aa3f0a5937:
Done when:

  • you can explain every field of a PreToolUse input and output;
  • you've seen each of the five anti-patterns fail, and can name the root cause;
  • you know which of the failure modes in section 10 fail open and which fail closed;
  • your mutation check turns a test red when you remove the gate.
